title: The month of Vaisakh
hook: in Vaisakh, how can the separated be patient (Barah Maha, ang 133)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the month of Chet, and your line: chet: joy. Did your seed go in? It's a week's end too: Guru Angad's voice, singing at dawn, the Asa di Var's close, a year of longing, separated by our deeds, Chet. Today, the second month, and the ache gets sharper. Day five hundred sixty-seven.
screen: `CHET: JOY.` · `A WEEK: THE DAWN VAR ENDS, THE MONTHS BEGIN.`

segments.voice: Vaisakh is harvest month in Punjab: April into May. The wheat is cut and threshed, the grain goes to market, and for a farming family it's a well-fed, busy, crowded time. Fairs come to the villages. Vaisakhi, the festival, falls in this month, and for Sikhs it carries the memory of the Vaisakhi when Guru Gobind Singh created the Khalsa. Everyone is home. Everyone is celebrating. And in the folk songs, that's what makes it a hard month to be the one whose beloved is missing.
screen: `HARVEST, APRIL INTO MAY.` → `VAISAKHI, AND THE KHALSA.` → `A HARD MONTH TO BE ALONE.`

segments.voice: The Vaisakh stanza is on ang 133, and it opens with a question. In paraphrase: in Vaisakh, how can the brides be patient, the ones separated from love? Dheeran, patience, steadiness. How can anyone hold steady when everyone around them is with the one they love? Then Guru Arjan names why the bride is alone. She has forgotten the Lord, the true Friend, and clung to maya, the world's deceptive glitter. And he names what she's clinging to. Sons, wife, wealth: none of them go along with you at the end. Only the One is imperishable. Entangled in false busy-ness, the stanza says, the whole world is wearing itself out. Notice the timing. This is harvest month. The grain is in. The money's coming. Guru Arjan isn't against any of that; Sikhs are householders, and earning honestly is part of the path. But the fullest month of the year is also an easy month to forget the One entirely. Plenty can be loud. Then the stanza turns. Vaisakh becomes beautiful, it says, when a holy person brings you to meet the Lord. The same harvest, the same festival, the same crowded house, become lovely once the missing one is found. So the ache isn't the end of the stanza. It's the door. The longing is a kind of compass needle: it points to what's missing. A person who never felt it might never look. Vaisakh is the month of having almost everything, and the stanza asks gently what the almost is.
screen: `HOW CAN THE SEPARATED BE PATIENT?` · `CLINGING TO MAYA, FORGETTING THE FRIEND.` · `PLENTY CAN BE LOUD.` · `BEAUTIFUL WHEN THE LORD IS MET.` · then, large: `VAISAKH: LONGING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: call someone you miss. Sit for a moment first. Breathe, and let one person come to mind whose absence you feel, someone still living and reachable, whom you haven't spoken to in too long. Picture their voice. Let yourself feel the missing, plainly, the way the stanza does. Then decide: after the bell, you'll call them, or send a message if a call isn't possible. Hold that intention for a few breaths. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for them. The bell holds the time.
The month of Vaisakh. Harvest and festival, when the separated bride can't hold steady, and the month becomes beautiful only when the Beloved is met.
Your line: vaisakh: longing. Today, make the call you planned. And at your fullest moment today, ask what the almost is. Day five hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: On the sangrand of Vaisakh, gurdwaras that keep the day read the Vaisakh stanza of the Barah Maha, and Sikhs celebrate Vaisakhi in this month, remembering the founding of the Khalsa.

fork.setup: it's Vaisakh, the grain is in, the house is full, and still you feel something missing. what does the stanza say makes the month beautiful?
options: meeting the Lord, through a holy person.
fork.reveal: Vaisakh becomes beautiful, the stanza says, when a holy person brings you to meet the Lord. the longing is the door.

original.note: Gurmukhi: in Vaisakh, the harvest month; the stanza's first word.

trapdoor: what you thought: a harvest poem.
what it means: a full month makes it easy to forget the One, and the ache of missing is the door to meeting.
what a scholar hears: dheeran opens the stanza; sons, wife and wealth are named as what doesn't go along, and the close turns on meeting the saint.
